definitions: Work in Q[u]. A root has multiplicity m when (u−α)^m divides f and the next power does not.

definitions: A polynomial f in Z[x] is primitive when its coefficients have gcd one. Reduction modulo a prime p preserves its degree if p does not divide the leading coefficient.

result.proof: Gauss’s lemma turns a nontrivial rational factorization into f=gh with primitive integer factors of positive degree. title: Perfect-power images admit complete valuation parametrizations
status: Classical mathematics or a newly chosen finite model developed with proof; historical claims delimited
summary: The recovered power-chart examples admit global elementary proofs. Prime valuations establish surjectivity of the parametrization; substitution alone would show only that a proposed family gives some solutions. definitions: For a nonzero integer a and a prime p, v_p(a) is the exponent of p in |a|.

result.name: Complete cusp parametrizations
result.statement: x²=y³ if and only if (x,y)=(t³,t²) for a unique t∈Z. Also 2x²=3y³ if and only if (x,y)=(18t³,6t²) for a unique t∈Z.

At p=3, 2a=1+3b gives b=2s+1 and a=3s+2. Every other prime again has valuations (3a_p,2a_p). Extracting these factors yields |x|=18u³ and y=6u², where u≥1 is an integer. The sign of x determines t=±u. Conversely, direct substitution gives 2·18²t⁶=3·6³t⁶, so the parametrization is exact.

example.setup: Invert a concrete point and impose an arithmetic restriction.
example.calculation: For (x,y)=(−144,24), x/18=−8 gives t=−2, and 6t²=24 checks the other coordinate. Restricting y≤150 gives |t|≤5, hence exactly eleven solutions including zero. The first equation forces b even, b=2r, and then a=10−3r≥0, so r=0,1,2,3. The second similarly gives d=2s and c=6−3s≥0, so s=0,1,2. These choices are independent and unique, producing 4·3=12 solutions. title: Superelliptic genus follows from finite and infinite ramification
status: Classical mathematics or a newly chosen finite model developed with proof; historical claims delimited
summary: The source gives a superelliptic genus formula and its Gauss–Bonnet counterpart. Both become rigorous on the smooth compact normalization of a squarefree equation. The point at infinity must be included: overlooking its gcd contribution changes the genus.
definitions: Let P∈C[x] be squarefree of degree m≥1, let d≥2, and let C be the smooth projective normalization of yᵈ=P(x). Set δ=gcd(d,m).
The map x:C→P¹ has degree d. Curvature below is the Gaussian curvature of any smooth Riemannian metric on the compact oriented surface C.

result.name: Genus, curvature and branch monodromy
result.statement: g(C)=[(d−1)(m−1)−δ+1]/2 and ∫_C K dA=2π[d+δ−m(d−1)]. Around a simple zero of P, analytic continuation multiplies a local branch of y by exp(2πi/d).
result.proof: Near a simple zero a, write P(x)=(x−a)u(x), u(a)≠0. A holomorphic dth root of u exists locally, so a local parameter t can be chosen with x−a=tᵈ. The ramification index is d, contributing d−1 at each of the m finite branch points. At infinity the equation has orders d·ord(y)=m·ord(x); dividing by δ shows that there are δ points above infinity, each with ramification index d/δ. Their total contribution is d−δ. Riemann–Hurwitz gives 2g−2=−2d+m(d−1)+(d−δ)=m(d−1)−d−δ, which rearranges to the stated formula. Gauss–Bonnet gives ∫K=2π(2−2g), yielding the curvature expression. definitions: Let Ω⊆{0,1}ⁿ be a finite nonempty population ordered lexicographically with 0 before 1. For a prefix q, let C(q) count its feasible completions.
